title: Course setup
text:
1. Environment

Ensure you have the latest compatible versions of RStudio and R installed for your computer. If you have not previously used R/RStudio, you can install them using the Self-Service desktop application or by reaching out directly to JAX IT.
Make sure you have the following packages installed. Simply copy the code chunk and run it in the RStudio console:


install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",
  "factoextra",
  "Rtsne",
  "uwot",
  "patchwork",
  "Seurat"
))

If Seurat doesn’t install correctly, you can install it through BioConductor as follows:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("Seurat")

That should do the trick!

To make sure the packages installed correctly, go ahead and try loading them in by running the following in the console:


library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(Rtsne)
library(uwot)
library(patchwork)
library(Seurat)

title: Course setup
text:
2. Data
We will be using the same dataset throughout the course. The original study sequenced 2,700 peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a healthy donor, which is freely available as the PBMC3k dataset from 10X Genomics.
A light-weight subset of this dataset is available as pbmc_small, which contains expression data for 200+ genes measured for 80 cells. utilizing a subset of the data helps ensure that all code can be easily and quickly run on most participants’ systems locally.
You do not need to download this dataset ahead of class, as it can be accessed after loading the Seurat package in our session.

title: Module 5: Practical interpretation
text:
Dimensionality reduction aids visualizations and insights into your data, but interpreting them correctly requires careful thought. This module focuses on how to critically evaluate results and avoid common pitfalls.
What you’ll explore:

How to interpret clustering and embedding plots

How preprocessing choices influence results

How to identify potential artifacts such as batch effects

What questions to ask when evaluating biological data

title: Module 3: Need for dimensionality reduction
text:
Biological datasets often contain thousands of features, making them difficult to visualize and interpret directly. Dimensionality reduction provides a way to summarize this information while preserving important patterns.
What you’ll explore:

Why dimensionality reduction is needed

How Principal Component Analysis (PCA) summarizes variation in data

title: Module 1: Understanding biological data structure
text:
Biological datasets are often high-dimensional and can be represented using familiar mathematical structures such as vectors and matrices. In this module, we will focus on how to interpret biological data in this framework and how to compare samples based on their features.
What you’ll explore:

What rows and columns represent in a biological dataset

How to think of samples (cells) as vectors

How similarity and distance between samples are defined

How clustering methods group similar samples

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Course description
This is an interactive pilot workshop aimed at strengthening foundational linear algebra concepts in the context of biological data analysis. The focus will largely be on gaining an intuitive understanding of how biological data is structured and transformed in modern analysis workflows, including clustering and dimensionality reduction methods like PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP. Participants will learn how to critically evaluate their data, choose appropriate analytical methods, and derive biologically meaningful interpretations. This course is aimed at researchers seeking a conceptual understanding of the framework typically implemented in analyzing biological data. Open to all skill levels.


Prerequisites
Intro to R I and Intro to Biostatistics I preferred but not required.



Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Represent biological data as vectors and matrices
Interpret similarity and distance between samples
Understand how transformations affect data structure
Understand the need for dimensionality reduction
Explain the biological significance of computing eigenvectors and eigenvalues
Distinguish between popularly used dimensionality reduction techniques
Identify appropriate methods/techniques for specific use cases
Critically evaluate plots in practice




Course structure
The course has been divided into 5 modules and an optional take-home activity as follows:
Module 1: Understanding biological data structure
Biological data is often high-dimensional and can be represented using linear algebraic structures such as vectors and matrices. This module introduces how to think about biological datasets in terms of samples, features, and similarity.
Module 2: Data transformations
Preprocessing steps such as normalization, centering, and scaling can substantially change how data is represented and interpreted. This module explores how these transformations impact data structure and downstream analysis.
Module 3: Dimensionality reduction
High-dimensional datasets are difficult to visualize and interpret directly. This module introduces dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), focusing on intuitive interpretation and the biological meaning of principal components.
Module 4: Beyond PCA
While PCA captures global structure, it may not fully resolve complex patterns in high-dimensional data. This module introduces nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods such as UMAP and t-SNE, and discusses how they differ from PCA.
Module 5: Practical interpretation
This module focuses on interpreting real-world results. Participants will learn how to evaluate plots, identify potential artifacts (e.g., batch effects), and determine which analytical methods are appropriate for different datasets.
Optional: Exploratory analysis
Participants can apply the concepts learned in the workshop to analyze a new dataset, exploring its structure and drawing informed conclusions about underlying biological patterns.

title: Module 4: Expanding beyond the PCA
text:
While PCA is widely used, it may not always capture complex structure in high-dimensional data. Other methods, frequently using non-linear modeling, can highlight different aspects of the data.
What you’ll explore:

How PCA compares to methods like UMAP and t-SNE

The difference between global and local structure

How different methods represent patterns in the data

When different dimensionality reduction approaches are useful

text:
Goal
By the end of this module, participants should understand:

biological data as a matrix

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Load dataset

options(timeout = 300) # Increases timeout to 5 minutes
SeuratData::InstallData("pbmc3k")


SeuratData::InstallData("pbmc3k")
pbmc <- SeuratData::LoadData("pbmc3k")

Instructor note:
Use a preprocessed PBMC3k object for the workshop. Avoid making participants run the full Seurat preprocessing workflow unless this is explicitly part of the course.

pbmc <- readRDS("data/pbmc3k_clean.rds")
pbmc

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Inspect metadata

head(pbmc@meta.data)


table(pbmc$seurat_annotations)

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What does one row in the metadata represent?
What kinds of information do we have about each cell?
Which variables are biological labels?
Which variables might be technical?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Extract expression matrix

expr <- GetAssayData(pbmc, assay = "RNA", layer = "data")
expr[1:5, 1:5]


dim(expr)

Instructor note:
Seurat stores this matrix as:
genes × cells
For most of our linear algebra intuition, it is easier to think in terms of:
cells × genes
So we transpose the matrix.

expr_t <- t(as.matrix(expr))
dim(expr_t)

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What does one row represent now?
What does one column represent now?
What is one cell represented as mathematically?

Answer:
Each cell is a vector of gene expression values.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Select variable genes
Instructor note:
We do not need every gene for teaching. Using all genes slows things down and adds noise.

variable_genes <- VariableFeaturePlot(pbmc)[1:1000]
expr_var <- expr_t[, variable_genes]

dim(expr_var)

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
section: Visualize a small part of the matrix
text:
Visualize a small part of the matrix

expr_small <- expr_var[1:10, 1:10]
expr_small

Instructor pause:
Ask:

Is this a small matrix or a slice of a larger matrix?
What would a row vector mean?
What would a column vector mean?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Look at expression distribution

expr_long_sample <- expr_var[
  sample(rownames(expr_var), 300),
  sample(colnames(expr_var), 50)
] %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("cell") %>%
  pivot_longer(-cell, names_to = "gene", values_to = "expression")

ggplot(expr_long_sample, aes(x = expression)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of expression values",
    x = "Log-normalized expression",
    y = "Count"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

Are most values high or low?
What does this suggest about biological data?
Is this matrix dense or sparse-ish?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Subset cells for distance calculations
Instructor note:
Pairwise distances across all cells can be slow and visually overwhelming. Use a subset.

cell_subset <- sample(rownames(expr_var), 250)
expr_subset <- expr_var[cell_subset, ]

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Compute distances between cells

cell_dist <- dist(expr_subset, method = "euclidean")
cell_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(cell_dist)

cell_dist_matrix[1:5, 1:5]

Instructor explanation:
Each value represents how far apart two cells are based on their gene expression vectors.
Instructor pause:
Ask:

What does a distance of 0 mean?
Why is the diagonal 0?
Why is the matrix symmetric?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Hierarchical clustering

hc <- hclust(cell_dist)

plot(hc, labels = FALSE, main = "Hierarchical clustering of cells")

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What is being clustered?
What information was used to cluster cells?
Do we know yet whether these clusters are biologically meaningful?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Heatmap of cell distances

heatmap(
  cell_dist_matrix,
  Rowv = as.dendrogram(hc),
  Colv = as.dendrogram(hc),
  scale = "none",
  labRow = FALSE,
  labCol = FALSE,
  main = "Cell-cell distance matrix"
)

Instructor note:
This is a good moment to connect:

similarity
distance
clustering
visual structure

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Goal
By the end of this module, participants should understand:

centering
scaling
why preprocessing changes data geometry
why transformations affect downstream analyses

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Gene means and variances

gene_summary <- tibble(
  gene = colnames(expr_var),
  mean_expression = apply(expr_var, 2, mean),
  variance = apply(expr_var, 2, var),
  sd = apply(expr_var, 2, sd)
)

head(gene_summary)


ggplot(gene_summary, aes(x = mean_expression, y = variance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean expression vs variance",
    x = "Mean expression",
    y = "Variance"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

Do all genes vary equally?
Why might highly variable genes dominate analyses?
Is high variance always biological?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Center data

expr_centered <- scale(expr_var, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

Check one gene before and after centering:

example_gene <- colnames(expr_var)[1]

mean(expr_var[, example_gene])
mean(expr_centered[, example_gene])

Instructor explanation:
Centering shifts each gene so its mean is 0.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Scale data

expr_scaled <- scale(expr_var, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

Check one gene before and after scaling:

sd(expr_var[, example_gene])
sd(expr_scaled[, example_gene])

Instructor explanation:
Scaling makes each gene have standard deviation 1.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
section: Compare raw, centered, and scaled values
text:
Compare raw, centered, and scaled values

compare_gene_df <- tibble(
  cell = rownames(expr_var),
  raw = expr_var[, example_gene],
  centered = expr_centered[, example_gene],
  scaled = expr_scaled[, example_gene]
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cell, names_to = "version", values_to = "value")

ggplot(compare_gene_df, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~ version, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = paste("Effect of centering and scaling on", example_gene),
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What changed after centering?
What changed after scaling?
Did the relative ordering of cells change for this gene?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Goal
By the end of this module, participants should understand:

why high-dimensional data is hard to visualize
PCA as a rotation of the data
PCs as directions of variation
variance explained
loadings as gene contributions

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Run PCA on unscaled data

pca_unscaled <- prcomp(expr_var, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)


pca_unscaled_df <- as_tibble(pca_unscaled$x[, 1:2], rownames = "cell") %>%
  left_join(
    pbmc@meta.data %>% rownames_to_column("cell"),
    by = "cell"
  )


ggplot(pca_unscaled_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA on centered, unscaled data",
    color = "Cell type"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What structure do we see?
Are cell types separated?
What might dominate this PCA?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Run PCA on scaled data

pca_scaled <- prcomp(expr_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)


pca_scaled_df <- as_tibble(pca_scaled$x[, 1:2], rownames = "cell") %>%
  left_join(
    pbmc@meta.data %>% rownames_to_column("cell"),
    by = "cell"
  )


ggplot(pca_scaled_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA on scaled data",
    color = "Cell type"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

How did scaling change the PCA?
Which version is easier to interpret?
Does scaling always make things better?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
section: Compare PCA with and without labels
text:
Compare PCA with and without labels

ggplot(pca_scaled_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "PCA without cell-type labels")


ggplot(pca_scaled_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA with cell-type labels",
    color = "Cell type"
  )

Instructor note:
This is a good place to emphasize:

Dimensionality reduction does not know the labels.
We add labels afterward to interpret the structure.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Variance explained

variance_explained <- pca_scaled$sdev^2 / sum(pca_scaled$sdev^2)

variance_df <- tibble(
  PC = seq_along(variance_explained),
  variance_explained = variance_explained
)

ggplot(variance_df[1:30, ], aes(x = PC, y = variance_explained)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Variance explained by principal components",
    x = "Principal component",
    y = "Proportion of variance explained"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

Why does PC1 explain the most variance?
Why do later PCs explain less?
How many PCs would you keep?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Cumulative variance explained

variance_df <- variance_df %>%
  mutate(cumulative_variance = cumsum(variance_explained))

ggplot(variance_df[1:50, ], aes(x = PC, y = cumulative_variance)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative variance explained",
    x = "Number of PCs",
    y = "Cumulative variance explained"
  )

Instructor note:
In single-cell data, variance is often spread across many PCs.
This is normal and useful to discuss.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
PCA loadings

loadings_df <- tibble(
  gene = rownames(pca_scaled$rotation),
  PC1 = pca_scaled$rotation[, 1],
  PC2 = pca_scaled$rotation[, 2]
)

loadings_df %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(PC1))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)


loadings_df %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(PC2))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

Instructor explanation:
Loadings tell us which genes contribute strongly to a principal component.
Instructor pause:
Ask:

If a gene has a large loading on PC1, what does that mean?
Does PCA know which genes are biologically important?
How would we interpret these genes carefully?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Goal
By the end of this module, participants should understand:

PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE are all dimensionality reduction methods
PCA emphasizes global linear structure
UMAP and t-SNE emphasize local neighborhood structure
visualizations are tools, not proof

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Use PCs as input
Instructor note:
For UMAP and t-SNE, we usually do not use all genes directly.
We use top PCs as a lower-dimensional representation of the data.

pca_coords <- pca_scaled$x[, 1:20]
dim(pca_coords)

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Run UMAP

umap_coords <- umap(
  pca_coords,
  n_neighbors = 15,
  min_dist = 0.3,
  metric = "euclidean"
)


umap_df <- as_tibble(umap_coords, .name_repair = "unique") %>%
  rename(UMAP1 = ...1, UMAP2 = ...2) %>%
  mutate(cell = rownames(pca_coords)) %>%
  left_join(
    pbmc@meta.data %>% rownames_to_column("cell"),
    by = "cell"
  )


ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "UMAP of PBMC3k",
    color = "Cell type"
  )

Instructor pause:
Ask:

What looks different from PCA?
Are clusters more separated?
Does more separation mean more truth?

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Run t-SNE
Instructor note:
This may take a little longer. Pre-run if needed.

tsne_coords <- Rtsne(
  pca_coords,
  dims = 2,
  perplexity = 30,
  verbose = FALSE
)$Y


tsne_df <- as_tibble(tsne_coords, .name_repair = "unique") %>%
  rename(tSNE1 = ...1, tSNE2 = ...2) %>%
  mutate(cell = rownames(pca_coords)) %>%
  left_join(
    pbmc@meta.data %>% rownames_to_column("cell"),
    by = "cell"
  )


ggplot(tsne_df, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "t-SNE of PBMC3k",
    color = "Cell type"
  )

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
text:
Compare PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE

p_pca <- ggplot(pca_scaled_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "PCA", color = "Cell type") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_umap <- ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "UMAP", color = "Cell type") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_tsne <- ggplot(tsne_df, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = seurat_annotations)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "t-SNE", color = "Cell type")

p_pca + p_umap + p_tsne

Instructor pause:
Ask:

Which method separates clusters most clearly?
Which method is easiest to overinterpret?
Which method preserves global structure best?
Are distances between clusters meaningful in all plots?

section: Demo 2 · Which Genes Are Actually Informative? ⏱ ~3 min
text:
Demo 2 · Which Genes Are Actually Informative? ⏱ ~3 min

Concept: Variance tells us which genes differ across cells. Low-variance genes are flat — they contribute noise, not signal. This is why we select highly variable genes before PCA.


# ── Gene variance distribution ────────────────────────────────────────────────
gene_vars <- sort(apply(pbmc, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE)

var_df <- tibble(
  rank     = seq_along(gene_vars),
  variance = gene_vars,
  gene     = names(gene_vars)
)

top8    <- slice_head(var_df, n = 8)
bottom5 <- slice_tail(var_df, n = 5)

ggplot(var_df, aes(rank, variance)) +
  geom_line(color = "#028090", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = top8,    color = "#F96167", size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = bottom5, color = "#94A3B8", size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data  = top8, aes(label = gene),
    color = "#F96167", size = 3.5, nudge_x = 3, max.overlaps = 15
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Gene variance across cells",
    subtitle = "Red = most variable (informative).  Grey = near-zero variance (flat, useless for PCA).",
    x        = "Gene rank  (most → least variable)",
    y        = "Variance"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))














🔍 Ask the room




“What do the red genes tend to be?” → cell-type markers, biologically meaningful
“What happens if we feed ALL 230 genes — including the flat ones — into PCA?” → Noise accumulates; uninformative genes dilute the signal from the useful ones
“This is why tools like Seurat select ‘highly variable genes’ before PCA.”

section: Demo 3 · What Preprocessing Does to Your Data ⏱ ~5 min
text:
Demo 3 · What Preprocessing Does to Your Data ⏱ ~5 min

Concept: Centering and scaling change the geometry of the data — and therefore what PCA finds. Same cells. Three different views. Only the reference frame changes.


# ── Raw vs centered vs scaled: same two genes, three preprocessing steps ──────
gx <- "MS4A1"
gy <- "CD14"
if (!gx %in% colnames(pbmc)) gx <- colnames(pbmc)[which.max(apply(pbmc,2,var))]
if (!gy %in% colnames(pbmc)) gy <- colnames(pbmc)[order(apply(pbmc,2,var), decreasing=TRUE)[2]]

pbmc_centered <- scale(pbmc, center = TRUE,  scale = FALSE)
pbmc_scaled   <- scale(pbmc, center = TRUE,  scale = TRUE)

make_scatter <- function(mat, ttl, sub) {
  tibble(x = mat[, gx], y = mat[, gy], cluster = metadata$cluster) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, y, color = cluster)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.75) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(title = ttl, subtitle = sub, x = gx, y = gy) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 9))
}

p1 <- make_scatter(pbmc,          "Raw",              "Original log-normalized")
p2 <- make_scatter(pbmc_centered, "Centered",         "Subtract each gene's mean")
p3 <- make_scatter(pbmc_scaled,   "Centered + Scaled","Mean = 0, SD = 1 per gene")

(p1 | p2 | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Same 80 cells — three preprocessing choices",
    caption = "The point cloud shape is preserved. Only the axis scale changes."
  )














🔍 Ask the room




“What changed on the axes going from raw to centered?” → the origin shifted to the mean; spread looks the same
“What changed from centered to scaled?” → both axes now have the same range
“Does the relative position of the points change?” → no — same biology, different reference frame
“Why does PCA care about this?” → PCA uses variance to decide which directions matter. If one gene has 100× more variance than another, PCA ignores the smaller one entirely.

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
section: Demo 4 · The Scree Plot: How Many Dimensions Matter? ⏱ ~4 min
text:
Demo 4 · The Scree Plot: How Many Dimensions Matter? ⏱ ~4 min

Concept: PCA finds directions ordered by variance explained. The scree plot shows where signal ends and noise begins — the elbow.


# ── Run PCA ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
set.seed(42)
pca <- prcomp(pbmc, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

var_exp <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
cum_var <- cumsum(var_exp)
n_show  <- min(30, length(var_exp))

scree_df <- tibble(
  pc          = 1:n_show,
  var_pct     = var_exp[1:n_show] * 100,
  cum_pct     = cum_var[1:n_show] * 100
)

# elbow: first PC where drop < 1%
elbow <- min(which(diff(scree_df$var_pct) > -1)) + 1

p_scree <- ggplot(scree_df, aes(pc, var_pct)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = pc <= elbow), width = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#028090", "FALSE" = "#CBD5E1")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = elbow + 0.5, color = "#F96167",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = elbow + 1.2, y = max(scree_df$var_pct) * 0.88,
           label = "← elbow", color = "#F96167", hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5)) +
  labs(title    = "Scree plot — variance explained per PC",
       subtitle = "Teal bars = signal.  Grey bars = mostly noise.",
       x = "Principal component", y = "% variance explained") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))

p_cum <- ggplot(scree_df, aes(pc, cum_pct)) +
  geom_line(color = "#028090", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#028090", size = 2.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, color = "#F9C74F", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = n_show * 0.7, y = 82,
           label = "80% threshold", color = "#B8860B", size = 3.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title    = "Cumulative variance explained",
       subtitle = "How many PCs capture 80% of total variance?",
       x = "PCs (1 to k)", y = "Cumulative %") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))

p_scree / p_cum














🔍 Ask the room




“PC1 explains X% of variance. What does that mean in plain English?” → That much of all cell-to-cell variation in gene expression can be described by a single number per cell
“Where is the elbow? What do the grey bars represent?” → After the elbow, each PC adds very little — mostly noise
“If we kept only the teal PCs, what fraction of the total information would we retain?” → Point to the cumulative plot

section: Demo 5 · PCA Plot + What Drives Each PC ⏱ ~5 min
text:
Demo 5 · PCA Plot + What Drives Each PC ⏱ ~5 min

Concept: The PCA scatter shows cells in PC space. The loading bar chart reveals which genes define each PC — the biology.


# ── PCA scatter ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pca_df <- tibble(
  PC1     = pca$x[, 1],
  PC2     = pca$x[, 2],
  cluster = metadata$cluster,
  group   = metadata$group
)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = cluster, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title    = "PCA — PC1 vs PC2",
    subtitle = sprintf("PC1: %.1f%%  |  PC2: %.1f%%  of total variance",
                       var_exp[1]*100, var_exp[2]*100),
    x        = sprintf("PC1  (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
    y        = sprintf("PC2  (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100),
    color    = "Cluster",
    shape    = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))









# ── Top gene loadings for PC1 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
loadings_df <- as_tibble(pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "gene")

top_pc1 <- loadings_df |>
  mutate(abs_pc1 = abs(PC1)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_pc1)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(PC1 > 0, "Positive (+)", "Negative (−)"))

ggplot(top_pc1, aes(reorder(gene, PC1), PC1, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Positive (+)" = "#028090",
                               "Negative (−)" = "#F96167")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 15 gene loadings — PC1",
    subtitle = "These genes define the dominant axis of variation in the data.",
    x        = NULL, y = "PC1 loading", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.subtitle  = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        legend.position = "top")














🔍 Ask the room




“Look at the top positive genes. What cell type do they belong to?”
“What about the top negative genes — a different cell type?”
“So what is PC1 actually measuring biologically?” → It is contrasting two populations — this is the dominant biological signal in the data
“Each cell’s PC1 score tells you where it falls on that axis — high score = more of the positive cell type”




# ── Optional: colour PCA by QC — run if time permits ─────────────────────────
p_nc <- ggplot(mutate(pca_df, n_counts = metadata$n_counts),
               aes(PC1, PC2, color = log10(n_counts + 1))) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(title = "Colored by library size", color = "log10\ncounts") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)


p_nc +
  plot_annotation(

    caption = "If structure maps to library size: normalization issue. If it maps to % mito: QC issue. No mitochondrial % detected here."

text:
Demo 6 · Skip Preprocessing — Watch It Fail ⏱ ~3 min

Concept: This demo is designed to produce a worse result. Showing what breaks — and why — is the best way to make the preprocessing lesson stick.


# ── PCA without centering or scaling ─────────────────────────────────────────
pca_raw <- prcomp(pbmc, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
var_raw  <- pca_raw$sdev^2 / sum(pca_raw$sdev^2)

p_bad <- tibble(PC1 = pca_raw$x[,1], PC2 = pca_raw$x[,2],
                cluster = metadata$cluster) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title    = "No centering or scaling",
       subtitle = sprintf("PC1: %.1f%%  — often just library size",
                          var_raw[1]*100),
       x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_raw[1]*100),
       y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_raw[2]*100)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#F96167", size = 9))

p_good <- tibble(PC1 = pca$x[,1], PC2 = pca$x[,2],
                 cluster = metadata$cluster) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title    = "Centered + scaled",
       subtitle = sprintf("PC1: %.1f%%  — biologically meaningful",
                          var_exp[1]*100),
       x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
       y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#028090", size = 9))

(p_bad | p_good) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Why preprocessing matters",
    caption = "Left: PC1 often captures library size, not biology.\nRight: cell clusters separate along biologically meaningful axes."
  )














🔍 Ask the room




“PC1 explains a lot more variance in the left plot. Is that better?” → No — high variance on PC1 here means one technical signal dominates
“Why are points compressed into a line on the left?” → Without centering, PC1 points toward the mean expression profile — all cells project onto it
“This is exactly why every scRNA-seq pipeline centers before PCA.”

title: Linear Algebra for Biologists
section: Demo 7 · PCA vs UMAP vs t-SNE ⏱ ~5 min
text:
Demo 7 · PCA vs UMAP vs t-SNE ⏱ ~5 min

Concept: The same cells, three methods. Each preserves different structure. The biology is identical — the picture changes.


# ── UMAP and t-SNE on top PCs ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
set.seed(42)
n_pcs      <- min(10, ncol(pca$x))
pca_scores <- pca$x[, 1:n_pcs]

umap_res <- umap(
  pca_scores, n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.3,
  n_components = 2, verbose = FALSE
)

tsne_res <- Rtsne(
  pca_scores, dims = 2, perplexity = 10,
  max_iter = 1000, pca = FALSE, verbose = FALSE
)

ct <- metadata$cluster

p_pca <- tibble(x = pca$x[,1], y = pca$x[,2], ct = ct) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = ct)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title    = "PCA  (linear)",
       subtitle = sprintf("PC1: %.1f%% | PC2: %.1f%%",
                          var_exp[1]*100, var_exp[2]*100),
       x = "PC1", y = "PC2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 8))

p_umap <- tibble(x = umap_res[,1], y = umap_res[,2], ct = ct) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = ct)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title    = "UMAP  (nonlinear)",
       subtitle = "n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.3",
       x = "UMAP1", y = "UMAP2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 8))

p_tsne <- tibble(x = tsne_res$Y[,1], y = tsne_res$Y[,2], ct = ct) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = ct)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title    = "t-SNE  (nonlinear)",
       subtitle = "perplexity = 10",
       x = "tSNE1", y = "tSNE2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 8))

(p_pca | p_umap | p_tsne) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Same 80 cells — three methods",
    caption = "Input for UMAP and t-SNE: top 10 PCA scores.\nAll three show the same biology — with different visual emphasis."
  )














🔍 Ask the room




“Which method separates the clusters most clearly?” → usually UMAP or t-SNE
“In which plot could you say something about how different two clusters are?” → Only PCA, cautiously — distances in UMAP and t-SNE are not interpretable
“t-SNE clusters look very tight and separated. Does that mean those cell types are biologically very different?” → No — that is a property of the t-distribution used in the algorithm, not the biology

section: Demo 8 · Same Data, Different UMAP ⏱ ~3 min
text:
Demo 8 · Same Data, Different UMAP ⏱ ~3 min

Concept: Changing one parameter produces a visually different layout from identical data. The biology does not change. The picture does. This is why you should never over-interpret a single embedding.


# ── Three n_neighbors values, same data ───────────────────────────────────────
run_umap <- function(nn) {
  set.seed(42)
  res <- umap(pca_scores, n_neighbors = nn, min_dist = 0.3,
              n_components = 2, verbose = FALSE)
  tibble(x = res[,1], y = res[,2], ct = ct)
}

make_up <- function(df, nn) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = ct)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(title    = paste0("n_neighbors = ", nn),
         subtitle = "Same cells, same seed",
         x = "UMAP1", y = "UMAP2") +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position  = "none",
          plot.subtitle    = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 8))
}

(make_up(run_umap(5), 5) | make_up(run_umap(15), 15) | make_up(run_umap(30), 30)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "UMAP is sensitive to n_neighbors",
    caption = "Small: tight local clusters, may fragment.\nLarge: smoother, more global structure.\nBiology is identical in all three."
  )














🔍 Ask the room




“Do the clusters look the same in each plot?” → No — different shapes and separations
“Is the biology different?” → No — same 80 cells, same expression, same colors
“What does this mean when you see a single UMAP in a paper?” → You are seeing one parameter choice out of many possible layouts

text:
Demo 9 · The Batch Effect Trap ⏱ ~4 min

Concept: Technical variation can look exactly like biology. The group variable in pbmc_small mimics what a batch effect looks like — two plots, identical data, completely different story depending on what you color.


# ── Color the same PCA by cluster vs by group ─────────────────────────────────
# 'group' in pbmc_small is g1/g2 — not a true batch, but serves as a proxy
# to illustrate the concept visually

p_cluster <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title    = "Colored by cluster",
    subtitle = "Looks like clean biological separation...",
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100)
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))

p_group <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("g1" = "#028090", "g2" = "#F96167")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Same plot — colored by sample group",
    subtitle = "...but how much does the group drive the structure?",
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[1]*100),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_exp[2]*100),
    color = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))

(p_cluster | p_group) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Two color mappings — same embedding",
    caption = "The only difference between these plots is which metadata column is used to color the points."
  )














⚠ The key lesson



If you only ever color by cell type, you can completely miss technical variation driving your embedding.
Always color by batch, sample, library size, and QC metrics — not just cell type. The two plots above are the same 80 cells. Only the coloring changed.








🔍 Ask the room




“If I showed you only the left plot, what would you conclude?” → Clean cluster separation — the analysis looks great
“Now look at the right. What question does it make you ask?” → Is the separation driven by biology, or by which group the cells came from?
“In your own data: what is the equivalent of ‘group’ that you should always check?” → Sample ID, processing date, sequencing batch, operator, reagent lot

#setting seed for reproducibility.

                      n_components = 2, 
                      verbose = FALSE)

#running t-SNE.
pbmc_tsne_res <- Rtsne(pbmc_pca_scores, 
                       dims = 2, 
                       perplexity = 10,
                       max_iter = 1000, 
                       pca = FALSE, 
                       verbose = FALSE)

#plotting outputs.
plot_embed <- function(x, y, title, xlab, ylab, show_legend = FALSE){
  tibble(x = x, y = y, cluster = metadata$cluster) %>%
    
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = cluster)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(title = title, 
         x = xlab, 
         y = ylab) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = if (show_legend) "right" else "none")
}

p_pca  <- plot_embed(pbmc_pca$x[,1], pbmc_pca$x[,2], "PCA", "PC1", "PC2")
p_umap <- plot_embed(pbmc_umap_res[,1], pbmc_umap_res[,2], "UMAP", "UMAP1", "UMAP2")
